tip: 'Se me cayó el alma al suelo' – accidental 'se' ('se' + indirect object). Literally 'my soul fell to the floor on me'. The 'se me' removes agency.
'El no haber estudiado' – an article on a verb? Spanish turns whole events into nouns with 'el' + infinitive, where English must switch to -ing: 'not having studied'.
'Me flipa' borrows English 'flip (out)' and works like 'gustar' – the series flips YOU. Mainly Spain slang: perfect with friends, jarring with your boss.
'Si no llega a ser por' – colloquial alternative to 'si no hubiera sido por' for past counterfactuals.
'Echar' (throw) is Spain's delivery verb for abstract things: 'le echaron la bronca' = they literally threw the scolding at him. Very colloquial – use 'regañar' in formal speech.
'No fue sino ... cuando' = 'it wasn't until ... that' – it pins down the moment something finally happened.
Why 'es' for location here? Events take 'ser': 'la fiesta es en mi casa' = it takes place there. Only physical things use 'estar' for where they are.
No 'once they were' needed – Spanish drops it all. The participle goes first and agrees with its noun: 'hechas las presentaciones' = the introductions (once) made.
English says 'having lived'; Spanish slaps 'el' on an infinitive instead: 'el haber vivido' = the-fact-of-having-lived, a noun that can be the subject.
'The more' can pluralize! Here 'cuanto' agrees like an adjective: 'cuantos más años' (masc. plural years). English 'the' never changes; 'cuanto' matches gender and number.
'No es sino' + gerund + 'como' = 'it is only by ... that', an emphatic way to stress how something gets done.
Why 'le' AND 'a mi amiga'? Spanish doubles a named receiver with the pronoun 'le': 'le regalé a mi amiga'. Dropping 'le' sounds broken, not tidy.
Why 'está', not 'es'? Here 'está fabricado' reports the finished state; 'es fabricado' would narrate the act of making it. Labels describe results, so 'estar'.
Birthdays aren't 'turned' in Spanish – they're completed: 'cumplió ochenta y siete años' = she 'fulfilled' 87 years. That's why it's '¡feliz cumpleaños!'
English needs 'has been godmother'; Spanish uses plain present: 'es madrina desde que nació'. If it started back then and still holds, present tense covers it.
Spanish deflects blame with 'se': 'se me pasó por alto' = the detail 'slipped past' on its own – 'me' just marks the bystander it happened to. Not 'I missed it.'
Spanish doubles the object: 'a quienes LES conté' – 'les' repeats the 'to whom' already stated. Redundant to English ears, expected in Spanish.
English writes a blank check; Spanish hands you 'carta blanca' – a 'white letter': a blank page to fill in however you like. Same total freedom, no money image.
Two 'but's: 'pero' adds a contrast, 'sino' corrects after a negative. 'No es empezar, SINO mantener' – whenever you mean 'not X but rather Y', only 'sino' works.
No 'the paradoxical thing' needed: 'lo paradójico' turns any adjective straight into an abstract noun. The same 'lo' works everywhere – 'lo bueno', 'lo raro', 'lo difícil'.
Five years and still counting? English needs 'has been living'; Spanish uses plain present: 'vive en el extranjero desde hace cinco años' – still true means present tense.
Nobody's to blame: 'Se nos pinchó una rueda' = the tire 'punctured itself on us'. Accidental 'se' recasts mishaps as things that happen TO you, not things you did.
'Es hablada' is grammatical but bookish: 'ser' + participle passives live in print. In conversation Spanish prefers the 'se'-passive – 'se habla español'.
Why the 'que'? Because a conjugated verb ('domina') follows. With a bare noun, 'sino' stands alone: 'no café, sino té'. Full clause after 'sino' = 'sino que', every time.
'Metí la pata' = literally 'I stuck my paw in'. Spanish's go-to phrase for a social blunder – and it's always 'pata' (an animal's leg), never 'pierna' (a human one).
'Firmado el contrato' – no 'once' or 'was' in sight. Fronting a bare participle means 'once X was done'. Formal shorthand beloved of contracts and news reports.
'Con que' here isn't 'with what': 'con que' + subjunctive ('se porten bien') means 'as long as' – the bare minimum you'll settle for, hence 'me conformo'.
Why not 'verde clara' to agree with 'la sudadera'? Compound shades like 'verde claro' are frozen – add 'claro' or 'oscuro' and the color stops agreeing entirely.
Past cause, present result: 'hubiera aprendido' (back then) pairs with 'no podría' (today) – Spanish mixes conditional timelines when a past event still affects the present.
Tempted by 'si me habrían invitado'? Spanish bans the conditional after 'si' – the if-half takes 'hubieran invitado'; only the result gets 'habría ido'.
